title: CoVA: Composing VAE Representations for Generative Learning

paper.title: CoVA: Composing VAE Representations for Generative Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Representation alignment with pretrained visual encoders improves diffusion transformer training but requires auxiliary encoders and extra training overhead. Recent approaches instead exploit representations from the generative model’s own variational autoencoder (VAE). However, reconstruction-oriented VAE features are not optimized for the semantic discrimination and spatial structure needed for generative learning. We introduce CoVA ( Co mposed VA E Representations), a lightweight framework that composes VAE features online into stage-wise guidance for flow-matching training. A small latent composer is jointly trained with class supervision, masked latent reconstruction, and horizontal-flip consistency, yielding semantically discriminative, spatially structured dense features and sample-dependent class posteriors. CoVA aligns intermediate SiT features with the composed representations early in training, then removes the increasingly detrimental alignment and reuses detached composer posteriors for sample-dependent soft label conditioning. We further uncover a hidden confound in soft label conditioning: averaging class embeddings attenuates their magnitude, coupling semantic interpolation with conditioning strength. This attenuation alone can substantially improve FID while degrading Recall, revealing a non-semantic source of the apparent gain. CoVA corrects this confound by restoring the hard-label magnitude, isolating posterior-dependent directional semantics. CoVA adds only 8.5M training-only auxiliary parameters (1.3% of SiT-XL/2) and introduces no inference-time overhead. On ImageNet 256 × \times 256, CoVA reduces SiT-XL/2 FID from 17.2 to 7.4 ( 57% ) in 400K steps. With classifier-free guidance, it achieves an FID of 2.03 in only 400 epochs, versus 2.06 after 1,400 epochs for vanilla SiT-XL/2.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in diffusion and flow-matching models have substantially reshaped modern image generation, delivering strong gains in visual quality, scalability, and training efficiency. From the original DDPM formulation Ho et al. (2020) and accelerated sampling methods Song et al. (2020) to flow-matching objectives Lipman et al. (2022) and scalable transformer architectures such as DiT Peebles & Xie (2023) and SiT Ma et al. (2024) , these developments have steadily pushed the frontier of generative modeling. Yet recent evidence suggests that generation quality depends not only on the learning objective, but also on the structure of intermediate representations formed during optimization. Representation alignment methods such as REPA Yu et al. (2024) and its follow-up analyses Singh et al. (2026) have shown that explicitly regularizing intermediate generative features can accelerate training and improve generation quality. A common strategy is to align these features with representations extracted from pretrained visual encoders such as DINO Caron et al. (2021) or CLIP Radford et al. (2021) . While effective, this approach requires an additional visual backbone throughout training, introducing nontrivial computational and memory overhead. A natural alternative is to reuse representations available within the latent generative pipeline. Recent work has shown that VAE-derived features can provide effective intermediate supervision without relying on an external visual encoder Leng et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026a) . However, VAE representations are learned primarily for reconstruction rather than semantic organization Zheng et al. (2026) , and are therefore not necessarily optimal supervision targets for a generative transformer. This motivates a fundamental question: can reconstruction-oriented VAE features be lightly reorganized into representations that are better suited for generative learning? To address this, we introduce CoVA ( Co mposed VA E Representations), a lightweight framework that learns to compose VAE representations online during flow-matching training. CoVA augments the VAE features with a latent composer trained using complementary semantic and structural objectives, including class supervision, masked latent reconstruction He et al. (2022) , and horizontal-flip consistency. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , this lightweight composition transforms the weakly organized spatial structure of raw VAE latents into coherent, object-aligned representations. Motivated by the finding of iREPA Singh et al. (2026) that spatial structure is critical to effective representation alignment, we use these composed dense features as supervisory targets for an intermediate SiT layer through a lightweight projector. The composer is trained online alongside the generative model using signals available in the training pipeline, avoiding dependence on a pretrained DINO-style or CLIP-style teacher. Our experiments further reveal that even improved representation supervision is not uniformly beneficial throughout optimization. Composed VAE features provide clear gains during the earlier stages of training, whereas prolonged alignment eventually degrades generation performance, consistent with recent observations Wang et al. (2026b) on REPA. This suggests that representation guidance is better viewed as a stage-dependent signal than as a persistent constraint. It also raises a natural follow-up question: once explicit alignment ceases to help, can the semantic information learned by the composer still benefit the generator without constraining its internal feature space? CoVA addresses this by shifting the role of the composer from representation supervision to conditioning. At later stages, CoVA removes the intermediate alignment objective and reuses the composer’s detached class posterior for sample-dependent Soft Label Conditioning. The VAE-derived signal thus evolves from shaping internal features to modulating class conditioning as training progresses. A closer analysis reveals a hidden confound in naive soft label conditioning. Forming a soft condition by averaging class embeddings changes two factors simultaneously: its semantic direction and its magnitude. The latter unintentionally alters the strength of class conditioning, making it difficult to distinguish gains from semantic interpolation from those caused by weaker or stronger conditioning. Empirically, naive soft conditioning lowers FID Heusel et al. (2017) and improves Precision, but also reduces Recall Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) , revealing a clear quality–diversity trade-off. Controlled ablations show that this trade-off is largely driven by the unintended magnitude change. CoVA therefore explicitly restores the condition magnitude, removing this confounding effect and allowing the posterior to contribute primarily through its sample-dependent semantic direction. CoVA introduces only 8.5M (1.3% of SiT-XL/2) training-only auxiliary parameters, including a 5.6M latent composer and a 2.9M alignment projector, incurs only 7.2% additional training-time GFLOPs, and is discarded at inference. Across SiT model scales, CoVA consistently improves generation quality under matched training budgets. On ImageNet, it reduces SiT-XL/2 FID from 17.2 to 7.4 at 400K steps, while reaching 2.03 with classifier-free guidance in only 400 epochs. These results demonstrate that VAE representations, when appropriately composed and reused across training stages, can provide effective generative supervision without auxiliary visual encoders. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We introduce a lightweight online latent composer that reorganizes reconstruction-oriented VAE latents into semantically discriminative and spatially structured dense representations, providing effective intermediate supervision without an external visual encoder. • Building on the stage-dependent nature of representation alignment, we show that VAE-derived information can play complementary roles across optimization. CoVA uses composed dense features for early representation shaping, then removes the feature constraint and later reuses the same composer through its detached, sample-dependent class posterior. • We identify a hidden magnitude confound in soft label conditioning: posterior averaging changes not only semantic direction but also condition magnitude, creating an unintended conditioning-strength shortcut. By restoring the hard-label magnitude, CoVA isolates the posterior-dependent directional signal and substantially mitigates the resulting fidelity–coverage trade-off.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Diffusion Transformers and Flow-Matching Models. Diffusion models have evolved from pixel-space denoising formulations Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) ; Kingma & Gao () ; Hoogeboom et al. () to latent generative models Rombach et al. (2022) , substantially reducing the computational cost of high-resolution synthesis. The adoption of transformer backbones Vaswani et al. (2017) ; Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) ; Bao et al. () ; Hatamizadeh et al. () ; Gao et al. (2023) ; Zheng et al. () ; Zhu et al. () has further improved scalability, leading to architectures such as DiT Peebles & Xie (2023) , SiT Ma et al. (2024) , PixArt- α \alpha Chen et al. (2024) , Stable Diffusion 3 Esser et al. (2024) , and Lumina Qin et al. (2025) . In particular, DiT establishes transformer-based denoising in latent space, while SiT generalizes this design to interpolant-based and flow-based objectives. Our work builds on SiT and focuses not on modifying the generative objective or backbone, but on improving how useful representations and conditioning signals are formed during training. Figure 3: Comparison between SRA2 and CoVA. (a) SRA2 aligns intermediate SiT features with VAE features through a lightweight projection layer and an auxiliary feature-alignment loss. (b) CoVA first composes clean VAE latents with an online composer trained by semantic and spatial objectives, and then reuses its dense features for early representation alignment and its detached class posterior for later soft conditioning. (c) CoVA’s stage-adaptive transition from representation alignment to soft conditioning enables faster training convergence and improved generation quality. Intermediate Representation Supervision for Diffusion Training. Recent work has shown that explicitly shaping intermediate representations can substantially accelerate diffusion-transformer training. REPA Yu et al. (2024) aligns intermediate diffusion features with representations from pretrained visual encoders, while subsequent studies further investigate which properties of the target representation are most beneficial for generation Singh et al. (2026) ; Wu et al. (2025) . In particular, iREPA highlights the importance of spatial structure in the alignment target rather than relying solely on global semantic quality Singh et al. (2026) . Although effective, these methods require pretrained representation encoders throughout training. Other approaches instead derive supervision internally. SRA Jiang et al. (2025) , DoD Yue et al. (2024) , and SSD Ma et al. (2025a) , for example, construct guidance from representations produced by the generative model or related teacher branches, reducing reliance on external foundation encoders. HASTE Wang et al. (2026b) further shows that representation alignment is strongly stage dependent: REPA provides substantial early benefits but can plateau or become detrimental when maintained later in training. CoVA shares the motivation of lightweight and stage-aware representation learning, but differs in both the source and the use of supervision: it first learns a task-adapted representation from VAE features and subsequently reuses the learned semantic information through class conditioning rather than maintaining feature alignment. VAE-Derived Representations for Diffusion Training. Variational autoencoders are fundamental components of latent diffusion systems, providing compact image representations that can be efficiently modeled by generative networks Rombach et al. (2022) ; Kingma & Welling (2013) . Existing studies have explored VAE-based improvements from two complementary perspectives. Latent compression methods Chen et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025b) reduce the spatial or channel redundancy of latent tokens to improve computational efficiency, while representation-oriented methods Yao et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Leng et al. (2025) aim to make the latent space more suitable for generation. For example, REPA-E Leng et al. (2025) jointly optimizes the VAE tokenizer and the latent diffusion model, whereas VAVAE Yao et al. (2025) investigates the tension between reconstruction-oriented representations and generation-oriented objectives. SRA 2 Wang et al. (2026a) demonstrates that VAE features can also provide effective visual guidance for diffusion transformers through a lightweight projection-based alignment objective, without introducing an additional large visual encoder or a second diffusion model. CoVA is most closely related to this direction, but differs in two important respects. First, rather than aligning the generator directly to raw reconstruction-oriented VAE features, CoVA learns a lightweight online composer that reorganizes them using semantic and structural objectives before they are used as supervision. Second, CoVA does not retain VAE-based feature alignment as a fixed training constraint: once alignment ceases to be beneficial, the composer’s classifier posterior is reused for sample-dependent class conditioning.

sections.text: Our method is built upon Scalable Interpolant Transformers (SiT) Ma et al. (2024) , which provide a common formulation for flow-based and diffusion-based generation. sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Experimental setup. We conduct all experiments on ImageNet Deng et al. (2009) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, following ADM preprocessing Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) . Images are encoded with the pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE Rombach et al. (2022) , yielding pre-extracted 4 × 32 × 32 4\times 32\times 32 latent codes. Unless otherwise specified, we use SiT-L/2 Ma et al. (2024) with 2 × 2 2\times 2 latent patches and train for 400 400 K iterations using SiT’s linear flow-matching path and velocity parameterization. SiT and the composer are optimized with AdamW Loshchilov & Hutter (2017) at a constant learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , zero weight decay, and global batch size 256 256 . We use EMA with decay 0.9999 0.9999 and mixed-precision training. The CoVA composer is a tiny ViT Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) block with width 192 192 , 12 12 Transformer blocks, 3 3 attention heads, and MLP ratio 4.0 4.0 , trained throughout the full 400 400 K iterations. We use label smoothing 0.1 0.1 , masking ratio 0.7 0.7 , MSE for masked latent reconstruction, cosine distance for flip consistency, and set all auxiliary loss weights to 1.0 1.0 . Following REPA Yu et al. (2024) , a token-wise MLP projector maps SiT features to the 192 192 -dimensional composer space. Features are extracted from blocks 4 4 , 8 8 , and 8 8 for SiT-B/2, SiT-L/2, and SiT-XL/2, respectively. The projector is a three-layer MLP with dimensions D → → → 192 D\!\rightarrow\!1152\!\rightarrow\!1152\!\rightarrow\!192 , with SiLU activations after the first two layers, where D D is the hidden dimension of the corresponding SiT backbone. Alignment is used for the first 200 200 K iterations, after which it is disabled and the detached composer posterior is used for SLC during the last 50K steps with replacement probability 0.9 0.9 and the magnitude correction from Sec. 3.3 . sections.heading: 4.2 System-Level Comparisons
sections.text: Comparison with SOTA methods. Tables 4.1 and 4.1 compare CoVA with representative generative models Chen et al. (2025c) ; Chen et al. (2025d) ; Wang et al. (2025) ; Ma et al. (2026) ; Li & He (2025) ; Ma et al. (2025b) and representation-alignment methods on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , without and with classifier-free guidance, respectively. Under the same 400K-step budget, CoVA consistently improves FID across SiT-B/2, SiT-L/2, and SiT-XL/2, from 33.0 to 21.4, 18.8 to 9.3, and 17.2 to 7.4, respectively. With CFG, CoVA achieves an FID of 2.03 and an IS of 316.4 in only 400 epochs, compared with 2.06 and 270.3 for vanilla SiT-XL/2 after 1,400 epochs. These results suggest that CoVA’s largest advantage appears in improving the underlying unguided generative model, while strong classifier-free guidance partially narrows the differences among training methods. We first isolate the contribution of each objective used to train the latent composer. As shown in Table 4 , masked latent reconstruction alone improves FID from 33.02 33.02 to 31.92 31.92 , while classification supervision alone further reduces it to 30.85 30.85 . Starting from classification supervision, adding masked reconstruction or horizontal-flip consistency yields comparable improvements, and combining all three objectives achieves the best FID of 26.83 26.83 , together with the highest IS and Precision. These results suggest that the objectives provide complementary supervision: classification organizes semantic information, while masked reconstruction and flip consistency preserve instance-level and spatial structure in the dense representations. Alignment Early Stopping. We next investigate how long the composed representation should be used as an alignment target. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), early stopping consistently outperforms full-training alignment, with stable performance across a broad stopping range: stopping alignment between 100 100 K and 250 250 K iterations yields FIDs between 26.42 26.42 and 26.64 26.64 , compared with 27.66 27.66 when alignment remains active throughout training. We therefore stop the representation-alignment objective at 200 200 K iterations in the subsequent experiments. SLC versus Fixed Label Smoothing. We then ask whether the benefit of soft conditioning comes from generic label smoothing or from the sample-dependent posterior produced by the online classifier. Under matched replacement probabilities, sample-adaptive SLC consistently outperforms fixed label smoothing, and the gap becomes more pronounced as the replacement probability increases, reaching 24.19 24.19 versus 28.29 28.29 FID at p = 0.9 p=0.9 in Fig. 4 (b). This result shows that the gain is not explained by weakening the hard condition alone. The instance-specific posterior provides additional useful information for generation. Since sampling uses hard-label conditioning, we cap the SLC replacement probability at p = 0.9 p=0.9 to retain sufficient hard-label exposure during training and limit the train–test mismatch. SLC Warmup Schedule. Finally, we study when the generator should start receiving the online classifier’s posterior. As shown in Fig. 4 (c), delaying SLC consistently improves performance across the tested schedules. We attribute this trend to the stage-dependent reliability of the posterior: early in training, the composer is still evolving and its predictions may provide unstable semantic mixtures that interfere with the formation of a robust hard-label-conditioned generative trajectory. Once the composer has matured, its posterior becomes more suitable as a sample-adaptive refinement of the class condition. We therefore enable SLC only during the final 50 50 K iterations.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented CoVA , a lightweight framework that reorganizes VAE representations and reuses them adaptively throughout flow-matching training. A small online composer first transforms reconstruction-oriented VAE features into more effective targets for intermediate representation alignment. As training progresses and explicit alignment becomes less beneficial, CoVA instead reuses the composer’s class posterior for sample-dependent soft conditioning. We further show that naive soft label conditioning entangles semantic interpolation with changes in embedding magnitude, and introduce a simple magnitude correction to remove this confounding effect. CoVA requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and introduces no inference-time component.

sections.heading: Masked latent reconstruction.
sections.text: To encourage the latent composer to preserve local and spatial information from the VAE representation, we adopt a masked latent reconstruction objective. We randomly mask a subset of latent tokens, denoted by ℳ \mathcal{M} , and use the composer to infer their representations from the remaining visible tokens. A lightweight prediction head D ⁡ ( ⋅ ) D(\cdot) maps the composed feature h i h_{i} at each masked position back to the VAE latent space. The reconstruction loss is defined as ℒ mim = 1 | ℳ | ​ ∑ i ∈ ℳ ‖ D ⁡ ( h i ) − Z i ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mim}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}\left\|D(h_{i})-Z_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (12) where Z i Z_{i} denotes the original VAE latent feature at position i i . The loss is evaluated only over masked positions, encouraging the composer to capture contextual and spatial structure rather than relying solely on local appearance.

sections.heading: Horizontal-flip consistency.
sections.text: We further impose a flip-consistency objective to encourage the composed dense representation to be equivariant to horizontal flipping. Given an input latent representation and its horizontally flipped counterpart, we obtain the corresponding composer features h h and h flip h^{\mathrm{flip}} . We then spatially flip h flip h^{\mathrm{flip}} back to the original coordinate system using ℱ − 1 ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\cdot) and minimize their cosine distance: ℒ flip = 1 N ​ ∑ i d cos ​ ( h i , ℱ − 1 ​ ( h i flip ) ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flip}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}d_{\cos}\left(h_{i},\,\mathcal{F}^{-1}(h_{i}^{\mathrm{flip}})\right). (13) Here, N N denotes the number of spatial tokens and d cos ​ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) d_{\cos}(\cdot,\cdot) denotes cosine distance. This objective encourages the composer to retain spatially consistent and transformation-equivariant information in its dense representations.

Composer features are the unmasked dense tokens before the classification head. sections.heading: Appendix D Understanding the Magnitude Confound in Soft Label Conditioning
sections.text: Geometry of soft class embeddings. We first analyze why posterior averaging systematically changes the magnitude of the class condition. Let { 𝒆 k } k = 1 K \{\bm{e}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} denote the learned class embeddings and let 𝒆 s = ∑ k = 1 K q k ​ 𝒆 k \bm{e}_{s}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}\bm{e}_{k} (14) be the naive soft condition produced from the composer posterior 𝒒 \bm{q} . For the trained SiT-XL/2 model, the class embeddings have similar magnitudes, with a mean L2 norm of 1.542 1.542 and a standard deviation of 0.180 0.180 . Meanwhile, different class embeddings are nearly orthogonal: the mean pairwise cosine similarity is only 0.016 ± 0.078 0.016\pm 0.078 . The squared magnitude of the soft condition can be written as ‖ 𝒆 s ‖ 2 2 \displaystyle\|\bm{e}_{s}\|_{2}^{2} = ‖ ∑ k q k ​ 𝒆 k ‖ 2 2 \displaystyle=\left\|\sum_{k}q_{k}\bm{e}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2} (15) = ∑ k q k 2 ​ ‖ 𝒆 k ‖ 2 2 + ∑ i ≠ j q i ​ q j ​ 𝒆 i ⊤ ​ 𝒆 j . \displaystyle=\sum_{k}q_{k}^{2}\|\bm{e}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}q_{i}q_{j}\bm{e}_{i}^{\top}\bm{e}_{j}. Since the class embeddings have comparable norms and small pairwise inner products, the cross terms in Eq. 15 are relatively small. Denoting the typical class-embedding norm by r ¯ \bar{r} , we obtain the approximation ‖ 𝒆 s ‖ 2 ≈ r ¯ ​ ∑ k q k 2 = r ¯ ​ ‖ 𝒒 ‖ 2 . \|\bm{e}_{s}\|_{2}\approx\bar{r}\sqrt{\sum_{k}q_{k}^{2}}=\bar{r}\|\bm{q}\|_{2}. (16) Therefore, posterior averaging naturally couples semantic uncertainty with conditioning magnitude. A concentrated posterior approaches the magnitude of a hard-label embedding, whereas a more dispersed posterior produces a shorter conditioning vector. Consequently, naive SLC changes not only the semantic direction of the class condition, but also its effective magnitude. Connection to classifier-free guidance. The sensitivity to condition magnitude can also be related to classifier-free guidance (CFG). Let 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 ) \bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}) denote the velocity prediction under condition 𝒆 \bm{e} , and let 𝒆 null \bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}} denote the unconditional embedding. CFG produces 𝒗 CFG = 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 null ) + w ⁡ [ 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 ) − 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 null ) ] , \bm{v}_{\mathrm{CFG}}=\bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}})+w\left[\bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e})-\bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}})\right], (17) where w w is the guidance scale. Locally linearizing the conditional prediction around 𝒆 null \bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}} gives 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 ) ≈ 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 null ) + 𝑱 e ​ ( 𝒆 − 𝒆 null ) , \bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e})\approx\bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}})+\bm{J}_{e}\left(\bm{e}-\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}}\right), (18) where 𝑱 e = ∂ 𝒗 / ∂ 𝒆 \bm{J}_{e}=\partial\bm{v}/\partial\bm{e} . Substituting this approximation into Eq. 17 yields 𝒗 CFG \displaystyle\bm{v}_{\mathrm{CFG}} ≈ 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 null ) + w ​ 𝑱 e ​ ( 𝒆 − 𝒆 null ) \displaystyle\approx\bm{v}(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}})+w\bm{J}_{e}\left(\bm{e}-\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}}\right) (19) ≈ 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , t , 𝒆 null + w ⁡ ( 𝒆 − 𝒆 null ) ) . \displaystyle\approx\bm{v}\left(\bm{x},t,\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}}+w\left(\bm{e}-\bm{e}_{\mathrm{null}}\right)\right). This provides a useful local interpretation of CFG as scaling the displacement of the condition from the unconditional anchor in embedding space. It does not , however, imply an exact equivalence between condition magnitude and CFG. The approximation is local, the soft condition is not generally collinear with the hard condition, and the limiting average class embedding does not coincide with the learned unconditional embedding. Moreover, the conditional response of a deep network is nonlinear, so 𝑱 e \bm{J}_{e} need not remain constant for large changes in condition magnitude. Nevertheless, Eq. 19 suggests that condition magnitude can act as an effective conditioning-strength coordinate. This is consistent with our inference-time scaling experiment, where directly rescaling a hard-label embedding substantially changes the fidelity–coverage trade-off even though all model parameters are fixed. Magnitude and direction play distinct roles. The analysis above explains why naive SLC contains an implicit conditioning-strength component, but does not imply that its directional variation is irrelevant. Our direction–magnitude decomposition in the main paper shows that replacing the hard-label magnitude with the attenuated soft magnitude produces a large improvement in FID, but also noticeably reduces Recall. This behavior indicates that magnitude attenuation primarily acts as a fidelity-oriented conditioning shortcut. In contrast, preserving the soft direction while restoring the hard-label magnitude yields a smaller but meaningful improvement while retaining substantially better coverage. Furthermore, shuffling soft directions across samples strongly degrades performance, demonstrating that the posterior-dependent direction contains sample-specific semantic information. Taken together, naive SLC entangles two fundamentally different effects: posterior-dependent semantic direction and posterior-dependent conditioning magnitude . The latter can strongly alter the fidelity–coverage balance and therefore confounds the apparent gain of soft conditioning. CoVA explicitly removes this confound by restoring the soft condition to the corresponding hard-label magnitude, while preserving its posterior-dependent direction. In this way, the soft condition contributes sample-specific semantic information without relying on unintended changes in conditioning strength. Null-centered controls for conditioning strength. Our default magnitude correction in Eq. (8) restores the soft condition to the norm of the corresponding hard-label embedding. Since the local interpretation of classifier-free guidance is more naturally expressed relative to the learned unconditional embedding 𝒆 ∅ \bm{e}_{\varnothing} , we further examine whether the observed effect depends on measuring magnitude from the origin. We conduct two complementary null-centered controls, one during training and one only at inference.

sections.heading: Null-centered normalization during training.
sections.text: For the naive soft condition 𝒄 ¯ j = 𝒒 j ⊤ ​ 𝑬 \bar{\bm{c}}_{j}=\bm{q}_{j}^{\top}\bm{E} , we construct a null-centered variant that explicitly preserves the distance from the learned unconditional embedding: 𝒄 j soft , null = 𝒆 ∅ + ‖ 𝑬 y j − 𝒆 ∅ ‖ 2 ‖ 𝒄 ¯ j − 𝒆 ∅ ‖ 2 + ϵ ​ ( 𝒄 ¯ j − 𝒆 ∅ ) . \bm{c}^{\mathrm{soft,null}}_{j}=\bm{e}_{\varnothing}+\frac{\left\|\bm{E}_{y_{j}}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right\|_{2}}{\left\|\bar{\bm{c}}_{j}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right\|_{2}+\epsilon}\left(\bar{\bm{c}}_{j}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right). (20) By construction, ‖ 𝒄 j soft , null − 𝒆 ∅ ‖ 2 = ‖ 𝑬 y j − 𝒆 ∅ ‖ 2 , \left\|\bm{c}^{\mathrm{soft,null}}_{j}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right\|_{2}=\left\|\bm{E}_{y_{j}}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right\|_{2}, (21) so the soft condition preserves the hard-label displacement from the unconditional anchor rather than only its norm with respect to the origin. Starting from the same 350K checkpoint, we replace the default normalization with Eq. 20 during the final 50K training iterations, while keeping all other SLC settings unchanged. As shown in Table 15 , null-centered normalization achieves an FID of 21.14 21.14 , closely matching the 21.45 21.45 FID of the default CoVA formulation. It also retains high Recall ( 0.628 0.628 ). This result indicates that the improvement from corrected SLC does not depend on using the embedding-space origin as the normalization reference ; preserving conditioning strength relative to the learned unconditional embedding leads to essentially the same behavior.

sections.heading: Null-centered scaling at inference.
sections.text: We next directly perturb conditioning strength relative to the unconditional anchor while keeping the model parameters fixed. For a hard-label embedding 𝒆 y \bm{e}_{y} , we define 𝒆 y ( γ ) = 𝒆 ∅ + γ ⁡ ( 𝒆 y − 𝒆 ∅ ) , \bm{e}_{y}^{(\gamma)}=\bm{e}_{\varnothing}+\gamma\left(\bm{e}_{y}-\bm{e}_{\varnothing}\right), (22) where γ = 1 \gamma=1 recovers the standard hard-label condition. This transformation changes only the displacement from the unconditional embedding and therefore provides a direct intervention on the conditioning-strength coordinate suggested by the local CFG interpretation. As γ \gamma increases from 1.0 1.0 to 1.35 1.35 , FID decreases from 24.87 24.87 to 9.19 9.19 and Precision increases from 0.58 0.58 to 0.71 0.71 , while Recall decreases from 0.64 0.64 to 0.56 0.56 . The same monotonic fidelity–coverage trade-off observed with origin-centered scaling therefore remains when conditioning strength is defined relative to 𝒆 ∅ \bm{e}_{\varnothing} . Together with the training-time control above, these results confirm that conditioning magnitude constitutes a genuine conditioning-strength coordinate rather than an artifact of origin-centered normalization , while the remaining gain of magnitude-corrected SLC is attributable to the posterior-dependent directional signal. Recent approaches instead exploit representations from the generative model’s own variational autoencoder (VAE). We introduce CoVA ( Co mposed VA E Representations), a lightweight framework that composes VAE features online into stage-wise guidance for flow-matching training. A small latent composer is jointly trained with class supervision, masked latent reconstruction, and horizontal-flip consistency, yielding semantically discriminative, spatially structured dense features and sample-dependent class posteriors. CoVA aligns intermediate SiT features with the composed representations early in training, then removes the increasingly detrimental alignment and reuses detached composer posteriors for sample-dependent soft label conditioning. We further uncover a hidden confound in soft label conditioning: averaging class embeddings attenuates their magnitude, coupling semantic interpolation with conditioning strength. This attenuation alone can substantially improve FID while degrading Recall, revealing a non-semantic source of the apparent gain. CoVA corrects this confound by restoring the hard-label magnitude, isolating posterior-dependent directional semantics. CoVA adds only 8.5M training-only auxiliary parameters (1.3% of SiT-XL/2) and introduces no inference-time overhead. On ImageNet 256 × \times 256, CoVA reduces SiT-XL/2 FID from 17.2 to 7.4 ( 57% ) in 400K steps. From the original DDPM formulation Ho et al. (2020) and accelerated sampling methods Song et al. (2020) to flow-matching objectives Lipman et al. (2022) and scalable transformer architectures such as DiT Peebles & Xie (2023) and SiT Ma et al. (2024) , these developments have steadily pushed the frontier of generative modeling. Yet recent evidence suggests that generation quality depends not only on the learning objective, but also on the structure of intermediate representations formed during optimization. Representation alignment methods such as REPA Yu et al. (2024) and its follow-up analyses Singh et al. (2026) have shown that explicitly regularizing intermediate generative features can accelerate training and improve generation quality. A common strategy is to align these features with representations extracted from pretrained visual encoders such as DINO Caron et al. (2021) or CLIP Radford et al. (2021) . While effective, this approach requires an additional visual backbone throughout training, introducing nontrivial computational and memory overhead. A natural alternative is to reuse representations available within the latent generative pipeline. Recent work has shown that VAE-derived features can provide effective intermediate supervision without relying on an external visual encoder Leng et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026a) . However, VAE representations are learned primarily for reconstruction rather than semantic organization Zheng et al. (2026) , and are therefore not necessarily optimal supervision targets for a generative transformer. This motivates a fundamental question: can reconstruction-oriented VAE features be lightly reorganized into representations that are better suited for generative learning? To address this, we introduce CoVA ( Co mposed VA E Representations), a lightweight framework that learns to compose VAE representations online during flow-matching training. CoVA augments the VAE features with a latent composer trained using complementary semantic and structural objectives, including class supervision, masked latent reconstruction He et al. (2022) , and horizontal-flip consistency. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , this lightweight composition transforms the weakly organized spatial structure of raw VAE latents into coherent, object-aligned representations. Motivated by the finding of iREPA Singh et al. (2026) that spatial structure is critical to effective representation alignment, we use these composed dense features as supervisory targets for an intermediate SiT layer through a lightweight projector. The composer is trained online alongside the generative model using signals available in the training pipeline, avoiding dependence on a pretrained DINO-style or CLIP-style teacher. Our experiments further reveal that even improved representation supervision is not uniformly beneficial throughout optimization. Composed VAE features provide clear gains during the earlier stages of training, whereas prolonged alignment eventually degrades generation performance, consistent with recent observations Wang et al. (2026b) on REPA. This suggests that representation guidance is better viewed as a stage-dependent signal than as a persistent constraint. It also raises a natural follow-up question: once explicit alignment ceases to help, can the semantic information learned by the composer still benefit the generator without constraining its internal feature space? CoVA addresses this by shifting the role of the composer from representation supervision to conditioning. At later stages, CoVA removes the intermediate alignment objective and reuses the composer’s detached class posterior for sample-dependent Soft Label Conditioning. The VAE-derived signal thus evolves from shaping internal features to modulating class conditioning as training progresses. A closer analysis reveals a hidden confound in naive soft label conditioning. Forming a soft condition by averaging class embeddings changes two factors simultaneously: its semantic direction and its magnitude. The latter unintentionally alters the strength of class conditioning, making it difficult to distinguish gains from semantic interpolation from those caused by weaker or stronger conditioning. Empirically, naive soft conditioning lowers FID Heusel et al. (2017) and improves Precision, but also reduces Recall Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) , revealing a clear quality–diversity trade-off. Controlled ablations show that this trade-off is largely driven by the unintended magnitude change. CoVA therefore explicitly restores the condition magnitude, removing this confounding effect and allowing the posterior to contribute primarily through its sample-dependent semantic direction. CoVA introduces only 8.5M (1.3% of SiT-XL/2) training-only auxiliary parameters, including a 5.6M latent composer and a 2.9M alignment projector, incurs only 7.2% additional training-time GFLOPs, and is discarded at inference. Across SiT model scales, CoVA consistently improves generation quality under matched training budgets. On ImageNet, it reduces SiT-XL/2 FID from 17.2 to 7.4 at 400K steps, while reaching 2.03 with classifier-free guidance in only 400 epochs. These results demonstrate that VAE representations, when appropriately composed and reused across training stages, can provide effective generative supervision without auxiliary visual encoders. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We introduce a lightweight online latent composer that reorganizes reconstruction-oriented VAE latents into semantically discriminative and spatially structured dense representations, providing effective intermediate supervision without an external visual encoder. • Building on the stage-dependent nature of representation alignment, we show that VAE-derived information can play complementary roles across optimization. CoVA uses composed dense features for early representation shaping, then removes the feature constraint and later reuses the same composer through its detached, sample-dependent class posterior. • We identify a hidden magnitude confound in soft label conditioning: posterior averaging changes not only semantic direction but also condition magnitude, creating an unintended conditioning-strength shortcut. By restoring the hard-label magnitude, CoVA isolates the posterior-dependent directional signal and substantially mitigates the resulting fidelity–coverage trade-off. 2 Related work Diffusion Transformers and Flow-Matching Models. Diffusion models have evolved from pixel-space denoising formulations Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) ; Kingma & Gao () ; Hoogeboom et al. () to latent generative models Rombach et al. (2022) , substantially reducing the computational cost of high-resolution synthesis. The adoption of transformer backbones Vaswani et al. (2017) ; Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) ; Bao et al. () ; Hatamizadeh et al. () ; Gao et al. (2023) ; Zheng et al. () ; Zhu et al. () has further improved scalability, leading to architectures such as DiT Peebles & Xie (2023) , SiT Ma et al. (2024) , PixArt- α \alpha Chen et al. (2024) , Stable Diffusion 3 Esser et al. (2024) , and Lumina Qin et al. (2025) . In particular, DiT establishes transformer-based denoising in latent space, while SiT generalizes this design to interpolant-based and flow-based objectives. Our work builds on SiT and focuses not on modifying the generative objective or backbone, but on improving how useful representations and conditioning signals are formed during training. (b) CoVA first composes clean VAE latents with an online composer trained by semantic and spatial objectives, and then reuses its dense features for early representation alignment and its detached class posterior for later soft conditioning. (c) CoVA’s stage-adaptive transition from representation alignment to soft conditioning enables faster training convergence and improved generation quality. Intermediate Representation Supervision for Diffusion Training. Recent work has shown that explicitly shaping intermediate representations can substantially accelerate diffusion-transformer training. REPA Yu et al. (2024) aligns intermediate diffusion features with representations from pretrained visual encoders, while subsequent studies further investigate which properties of the target representation are most beneficial for generation Singh et al. (2026) ; Wu et al. (2025) . In particular, iREPA highlights the importance of spatial structure in the alignment target rather than relying solely on global semantic quality Singh et al. (2026) . Although effective, these methods require pretrained representation encoders throughout training. Other approaches instead derive supervision internally. SRA Jiang et al. (2025) , DoD Yue et al. (2024) , and SSD Ma et al. (2025a) , for example, construct guidance from representations produced by the generative model or related teacher branches, reducing reliance on external foundation encoders. HASTE Wang et al. (2026b) further shows that representation alignment is strongly stage dependent: REPA provides substantial early benefits but can plateau or become detrimental when maintained later in training. CoVA shares the motivation of lightweight and stage-aware representation learning, but differs in both the source and the use of supervision: it first learns a task-adapted representation from VAE features and subsequently reuses the learned semantic information through class conditioning rather than maintaining feature alignment. VAE-Derived Representations for Diffusion Training. Variational autoencoders are fundamental components of latent diffusion systems, providing compact image representations that can be efficiently modeled by generative networks Rombach et al. (2022) ; Kingma & Welling (2013) . Existing studies have explored VAE-based improvements from two complementary perspectives. Latent compression methods Chen et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025b) reduce the spatial or channel redundancy of latent tokens to improve computational efficiency, while representation-oriented methods Yao et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Leng et al. (2025) aim to make the latent space more suitable for generation. For example, REPA-E Leng et al. (2025) jointly optimizes the VAE tokenizer and the latent diffusion model, whereas VAVAE Yao et al. (2025) investigates the tension between reconstruction-oriented representations and generation-oriented objectives. SRA 2 Wang et al. (2026a) demonstrates that VAE features can also provide effective visual guidance for diffusion transformers through a lightweight projection-based alignment objective, without introducing an additional large visual encoder or a second diffusion model. CoVA is most closely related to this direction, but differs in two important respects. First, rather than aligning the generator directly to raw reconstruction-oriented VAE features, CoVA learns a lightweight online composer that reorganizes them using semantic and structural objectives before they are used as supervision. Second, CoVA does not retain VAE-based feature alignment as a fixed training constraint: once alignment ceases to be beneficial, the composer’s classifier posterior is reused for sample-dependent class conditioning. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries Our method is built upon Scalable Interpolant Transformers (SiT) Ma et al. Therefore, the large gain of naive SLC cannot be attributed solely to semantic interpolation. 5 Conclusion We presented CoVA , a lightweight framework that reorganizes VAE representations and reuses them adaptively throughout flow-matching training. A small online composer first transforms reconstruction-oriented VAE features into more effective targets for intermediate representation alignment. As training progresses and explicit alignment becomes less beneficial, CoVA instead reuses the composer’s class posterior for sample-dependent soft conditioning. We further show that naive soft label conditioning entangles semantic interpolation with changes in embedding magnitude, and introduce a simple magnitude correction to remove this confounding effect. CoVA requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and introduces no inference-time component.
